title: The Symposium — Part One
subtitle: The dinner party. Plato, staged: everyone must praise Love.

customObject.name: the krater
customObject.description: the great wine-mixing bowl at the centre of the couches — tonight, mostly for show

script.note: MAP: the_hallwyl_museum_1st_floor_combined — a lamplit dining room standing in for Agathon's house, Athens. The evening after his first play won the prize. Couches around a low table; the krater in the middle.
Aristodemus hovers at the door — invited by Socrates, who has since vanished somewhere up the street.

script.text: Agathon — before you say anything — I know I wasn't invited. Socrates dragged me along and then simply… stopped. On your neighbour's porch. He's just standing there. Thinking.
Aristodemus! The gods send the guests the host forgot to ask for — come in, you're saving my table from an empty couch.
And someone fetch Socrates off that porch before the neighbours charge him rent.
Leave him. When Socrates stops to think, hauling him in early is like pulling bread out of the oven half-baked. He'll arrive when the thought does.

script.note: Laughter. Food is brought. Halfway through the meal, Socrates finally wanders in, entirely unbothered.

script.text: Forgive me. I was thinking. It happens where it happens — porches have no monopoly on wisdom, but they are rent-free.
Sit by me, Socrates — perhaps whatever you caught out there is contagious.
If wisdom spread by sitting close, Agathon, the wise would be very popular furniture. Alas — it has never once worked.

script.note: The plates are cleared. The moment arrives when, by custom, the serious drinking would begin. A collective, quiet dread crosses several faces.

script.text: Gentlemen. A show of hands — who here is still wounded from last night's drinking?
Wounded? I'm a casualty. If wine looks at me tonight I shall surrender to it unconditionally.
Then it's agreed — tonight we drink for pleasure, not for conquest. Light cups only.
And as a doctor, I prescribe it. Wine in victory is medicine; wine two nights running is a siege against oneself.

script.note: The flute-girl steps forward to play. Eryximachus raises a hand, kindly.

script.text: And let the flute-girl play for the women of the house tonight — or for herself. Because if we are not drinking, we shall need better entertainment: conversation.
Careful, doctor. In this room 'conversation' is a blood sport.

Then let us make it a fair contest. Here is my proposal. Of all the gods, one alone has never had a hymn worth the name — Love himself. Poets praise everything else under the sun. Eros they leave to amateurs.
So: each of us, in turn around the couches, shall give a speech in praise of Love. The finest speech wins the night. Phaedrus — the complaint was yours first. You begin.

script.note: OBJECTIVE — the contest of speeches begins. Phaedrus rises, young and entirely delighted with himself.

script.text: Then I say this: Love is the oldest of the gods — and the mightiest, because he alone makes us ashamed to be less than we could be.

A man will play the coward in front of his general, his father, his whole city — and stand and die rather than look small before the one he loves. No drill instructor on earth manufactures courage. Love does it for free.
Give me an army of lovers, each fighting under the eyes of the other, and that little army conquers the world. That is my praise: Love is the god who makes ordinary people brave.

script.note: Applause — some of it sincere. Socrates applauds one beat longer than everyone else, watching Phaedrus with interest.

script.text: A fine opening. Though I notice, Phaedrus, your Love does all his work through shame — a god of courage whose whip is embarrassment. I only mark the spot; someone will dig there later.
Later indeed — the order stands, Socrates, and you speak last. Pausanias, you're next: and no mercy, he's been rehearsing all week.

script.note: TO BE CONTINUED — Part Two: Pausanias divides Love in two — the common and the heavenly — and the night's real argument begins.
